title: Professional Skills, Lesson 3: Preparing for the modelling test and the case interview
subtitle: Time management, the order in which you build a model, and how to think out loud while working
whyItMatters: The modelling test is the real screening round for almost every analytical role. Most candidates fail it not for lack of knowledge but for mismanaging time - and that is something you can train.
openingQuestion: In a 90-minute modelling test, what should you do first?
openingOptions: Start entering historical figures immediately to make the most of the time available
Read the whole brief, identify the deliverable, then allocate the hours
Build the valuation first because it carries the most marks in the exercise
Set up the formatting and colour conventions for the whole workbook before entering numbers
explanation: The most common way candidates fail is by building the early sections meticulously and running out of time before reaching a final number. A rough model that runs and produces an answer always scores higher than a beautiful half-finished one, because the employer wants to know whether you can deliver under time pressure. Reading the brief first and working backwards from the deliverable is the simplest technique there is, and the most frequently skipped.

diagram.label: Read the brief, identify the final deliverable
Allocate the time backwards across each section
Build a working version first, refine afterwards
Keep the last 10 minutes for checking and a written conclusion

realWorldExample.description: The first candidate builds a highly detailed revenue schedule by product line, formats it beautifully, and runs out of time just as the income statement is finished. The second projects revenue on a single simple growth assumption, links all three statements, produces a valuation, and then uses the remaining time to go back and refine the revenue build and note the assumptions. The second candidate is chosen almost every time, even though their revenue section is cruder.

quiz.question: What is the principle for building a model under time pressure?
options: Copy the structure from a template model prepared before the test
Perfect each section as far as possible before moving to the next
Prioritise the valuation and skip the cash flow statement when short
Build a simple end-to-end working version first, then refine each part
quiz.explanation: This approach guarantees you have something submittable at any moment, and it also surfaces linking errors between sections early - the very errors that a section-by-section approach only reveals when it is far too late. Perfecting sequentially is what leaves candidates stranded, dropping the cash flow statement breaks the links the graders check first, and a memorised template rarely fits the brief in front of you.

quiz.question: Why should you think out loud in an observed case exercise?
options: Because the assessor grades the reasoning, and silence shows them nothing
Because the interview process requires candidates to narrate every single action
Because speaking aloud helps the candidate catch errors in their own arithmetic
Because the assessor needs notes on the steps to compare candidates with each other
quiz.explanation: A candidate who reaches the wrong number with coherent reasoning usually scores higher than one who reaches the right number and cannot explain why. It is not a procedural requirement and it is not primarily about catching your own slips or about the assessor's note-taking. In real work you always have to defend your number, not merely produce it.

quiz.question: When a piece of data is missing from the brief, what is the right way to handle it?
options: Stop and ask the examiner until you receive the exact figure needed
State your assumption clearly, note it in the model, and carry on
Skip the part that needs the data and move on to other sections
Use a random number since the aim is to complete the model structure
quiz.explanation: Missing data in a brief is usually deliberate, to see how you cope with incomplete information - exactly as in real work. Waiting for the examiner burns the clock, skipping the section leaves the model unlinked, and picking a number at random is only different from a stated assumption in one respect, which is the one that matters. Stating the assumption openly is the right answer; quietly choosing a number and saying nothing is the wrong one.

quiz.question: What should most of the final 10 minutes be spent on?
options: Add several more forecast scenarios so the model looks more complete
Reformat the spreadsheet and harmonise the colour conventions across sheets
Check that it balances, sweep for errors, and write a short conclusion
Recheck all the historical data entered at the start of the exercise
quiz.explanation: A model whose balance sheet does not balance is rejected outright no matter how good the rest is. Extra scenarios and tidy formatting add nothing when the core is unverified, and re-entering historical data at that point is the least likely place for a fatal error. A few lines of conclusion also show you understand what the number you just produced means - the part most candidates drop when the clock runs out.

quiz.question: Why do employers accept a rough but working model?
options: Because they assume the candidate will be trained further after joining
Because a rough model is easier to grade, saving the panel time
Because model detail does not matter much in real day-to-day work
Because it proves the candidate can deliver a finished product on time
quiz.explanation: In real work, deadlines are real and always earlier than you would like. Detail does matter on the job, grading convenience is not a design goal of the exercise, and nobody is counting on post-hire training to supply the basics. The ability to break work down so that a usable version always exists is a core professional skill, and the test is designed to measure exactly that.

keyTakeaways: Read the whole brief and allocate time backwards from the deliverable before typing into the first cell
Build an end-to-end working version first and refine later - do not perfect one section at a time
When data is missing, state the assumption clearly and note it; do not quietly pick a number
Keep the last 10 minutes for checking the balance sheet and writing a few lines of conclusion

practicePrompt.question: With 20 minutes left, your cash flow statement is not fully linked and the balance sheet does not balance. What should you do?
options: Keep fixing the links until they are right, accepting no time for valuation
Note what is unfinished, use a simple number to run on and reach a valuation
Delete the part that is out of balance so the model looks clean, then submit
Stop and explain to the assessor that the task is too long for the time given
practicePrompt.explanation: The assessor needs to see you carry the whole line of thinking through to a final result. An honest note saying the linking is incomplete and this is the temporary workaround shows you have the situation under control. Deleting the section that does not balance is the worst option of the four - it conceals rather than acknowledges.

summary.keyIdea: The test measures your ability to deliver under pressure, not the sophistication of the model
summary.commonMistake: Pouring time into the opening sections and running out before producing a final answer
summary.action: Time yourself for 90 minutes building a three-statement model with a valuation, and repeat it three times with three different companies.

application.title: A four-week practice plan
application.message: Week 1: build models with no time limit until the structure is second nature. Week 2: time yourself at 120 minutes. Week 3: 90 minutes. Week 4: 90 minutes while narrating your reasoning out loud, as though someone were watching.
application.secondary: The skill here is closer to sport than to academic study - it comes from the number of repetitions, not the number of pages read.

sections.text: The financial modelling stage taught you structure; the Excel stage taught you execution. This lesson is about the situation where both are tested at once against a countdown clock, and about why most people who fail do not fail on knowledge.

items: 10 minutes: read the brief, identify the deliverable, sketch the structure and the assumptions block
20 minutes: enter the historical data and build the revenue forecast at the simplest acceptable level
30 minutes: build the three statements and link them until the balance sheet balances
20 minutes: valuation and one or two scenarios
10 minutes: sweep for errors, check the balance, write a short conclusion

sections.label: The working-version principle
sections.text: At any point in the 90 minutes you should have a model that runs end to end, differing only in how polished it is. The approach is identical to the minimum viable product principle in software development, and for the same reason: it protects you from running out of time with something half-built.

left.label: What you think is being graded
left.text: The precision of every number and the granularity of the revenue forecast.

right.label: What is actually being graded
right.text: Whether the structure is clean, whether the three statements link correctly, how you handle missing data, and whether you reach a result inside the deadline.

lines: The modelling test does not measure knowledge; it measures working habits under pressure.
The final lesson of the stage steps back to view all of these skills within a career path.
